title: HIPC U19 Genomics Core
text: SUMMARY/ABSTRACT The Genomics Core will provide sample processing and next-generation sequencing for the BRI HIPC Center entitled “Systems immunology profiling of respiratory viral infections in vulnerable populations”. This core will serve both Research Projects, receiving samples from the Clinical Core, and sharing high quality ‘omics profiles with the Data Management and Analysis Core. The Genomics Core has two Specific Aims, In Specific Aim 1, the Genomics Core will process nasal, blood and sputum samples and then perform genome scale bulk RNA sequencing. In Specific Aim 2, the Genomics Core will perform single cell proteogenomic sequencing (Total-seq) of both global and antigen-specific populations to elucidate single cell transcriptomes, single cell immunophenotypes, and T cell receptor (TCR)/B cell receptor (BCR) clonotypes. For the global T cell analysis, the Genomics Core will utilize the 10X Chromium platform with 10X Single Cell Immune Profiling and BioLegend TotalSeq protocols for simultaneous single cell measurements of gene expression, cell surface antibody staining and TCR/BCR reconstruction. For rare autoantigen-specific populations where too few cells are available for use on the 10X system, the Genomics Core will utilize cell sorting on a flow cytometer into multi-well plates. In both cases, the Genomics Core will integrate transcriptomic and TCR/BCR clonotype measurements to link cells sharing ancestral relationships. The antigen-specific T cells to be examined is dependent on the project with Research Project 1 focused on allergen-specific T cells and Research Project 2 focused on citrullinated-antigen-specific T cells, implicated in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis. All transcriptomic data generated by the Genomics Core will be aligned to human and viral reference genomes and processed prior to transfer to the Data Management and Analysis Core for advanced analysis. The Genomics Core will work closely with each of the Project and Core Leads in the HIPC Center.

title: Structure and Function of an ADAM10-Tspan5 Complex
text:
A Disintegrin and Metalloprotease 10 (ADAM10) is an enzyme that catalyzes the ectodomain shedding of
critical signaling and adhesion proteins including Notch, amyloid precursor protein, and cadherins, and its
dysregulation is implicated in the development of varied pathologies including neurodegenerative diseases and
several cancers. ADAM10 is tightly regulated by the C8 subclass of tetraspanin proteins (TspanC8s) according
to mechanisms that are incompletely understood. This proposal aims to combine structural and functional
studies of an ADAM10-Tspan5 complex to elucidate mechanisms by which TspanC8s influence ADAM10
substrate selectivity.

title: The Center for Tumor-Immune Systems Biology at MSKCC
text:
The Center for Tumor-Immune Systems Biology at MSKCC
NARRATIVE
Cancer immunotherapies are designed to harness the human immune system to attack cancer cells and
eliminate tumors. Breakthroughs in cancer immunotherapy such as checkpoint blockade agents have
revolutionized cancer care, but only a fraction of patients with specific tumor types respond to these new
treatments. Our proposed Research Center will deploy tools from systems biology to improve our fundamental
understanding of tumor-immune interactions in contexts where current immunotherapies fail and to develop
novel strategies for enhancing responses in contexts where they have only partial success.

title: Lung Cancer Susceptibility in Deployed Gulf War Veterans
text:
Many of the ~700,000 military service members deployed during the Gulf War experienced deployment-related
respiratory exposures (DRREs) from burn pit combustion products, particulate matter, and chemical toxins.
These exposures are now presumed to be linked to the development of lung cancer and other respiratory
diseases. Yet, the mechanism by which DRREs in the Persian Gulf render Veterans susceptible to lung cancer
is poorly understood. Our findings in mouse models indicate that respiratory exposure to Gulf War Toxins induces
sustained inflammation in the lung, driven by alterations in how genes are expressed (epigenetics). We propose
to (1) study epigenetic changes in lung specimens from deployed Gulf War Veterans with lung cancer, (2) expose
mice to aerosolized gulf war toxins and determine the impact on developing cancer, and (3) reverse epigenetic
alterations in cancer causing pathways. If successful, these aims may lead to novel screening for Gulf War
Veterans at increased risk of developing lung cancer and potentially a way to reverse these changes.

title: Neurodevelopment of Tourette syndrome
text:
In the proposed continuation of this research, we will expand the postmortem tissue studies
to additional regions of the basal ganglia and cerebral cortex in a large collection of cases and
controls. Using basal ganglia organoids, and single cell transcriptomic, epigenomic and cell
lineage assays, we will map the differentiation and maturation of the various basal ganglia cell
types, elucidate the alterations in organoids from TS individuals and perform reversal
experiments to understand the sufficiency of key regulators in causing the TS phenotype. These
complementary experiments will define the likely time of origin, cellular and molecular
pathophysiology of TS and provide a disease model that can be used in future translational
studies.

title: Enriching and Base-Resolution Profiling of 5-Methylcytosine in Degraded Clinical Samples
text:
The epigenome carries ample cancer signatures, but their detection in clinical samples, such as formalin-
fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues and cell-free DNA (cfDNA), is hindered by the limited quantity and poor
quality of DNA. To overcome this challenge, we propose to map cancer-associated 5-methylcytosine, the most
abundant epigenetic modification in the human genome, through novel enzymatic conversions. Successful
launch of our technology will transform the clinical practice for epigenome profiling, facilitating mechanistic
studies using FFPE samples and expediting early cancer diagnosis using cfDNA.

title: Polysaccharide utilization and antimicrobial resistance in abundant gut bacteria
text:
The proposed project is relevant to public health because it will advance our knowledge of how abundant gut
bacteria obtain nutrients and resist antimicrobials, which is relevant to the NIGMS’s mission to increase our
understanding of biological processes and lays the foundation for advances in disease diagnosis, treatment, and
prevention. By using advanced methods and approaches from multiple disciplines, the research will give us more
knowledge about how microbes grow and survive in the gut. This could lead to new treatments and diagnostic
tests to improve gut health.

title: Neural circuit dynamics of spatial reward memory
text:
Rewarding experiences must be remembered clearly to guide healthy learning, but this memory process can be
disrupted in disorders such as dementia and drug addiction. To address our limited understanding of how the
brain amplifies the events surrounding reward in memory, this research will leverage large-scale recording
technologies to uncover the neural dynamics involved in forming spatial reward memories in two key brain
regions, the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex. By investigating what aspects of the rewarding experience are
stored and how they are stored, this work will enhance our knowledge of normal memory function and provide
insight into neural processes that could deteriorate in mental disorders.

title: Defining Distinct Mechanisms of Interferon Gamma Trained Immunity
text:
Trained immunity, the capacity of innate immune cells to retain memory of past stimuli, significantly impacts the
immune system's ability to combat infections. The mechanisms through which this memory is encoded remains
unclear. This proposal aims to delineate how interferon gamma, a key cytokine driving trained immunity,
utilizes distinct mechanisms to encode such memory in different innate immune cell types.

title: Genomic methods for studying microbial transmission in healthcare settings
text:
The spread of infections in hospitals represents a major risk to patients seeking care in healthcare facilities. In
this proposal we seek to develop, validate and apply strategies grounded in genomics to more effectively track
the spread of infections and thereby enable the development of better infection prevention strategies.

title: Pilot Studies on SCYL2, an AMC-Associated Protein, in Endocytosis and Neuronal Development
text:
SCYL2 is an understudied protein associated with the rare diseases Arthrogryposis Multiplex Congenita
type 4 (AMC4), characterized by multiple joint contractures and other neurogenic phenotypes, including brain
malformations. The proposed research aims to characterize the endogenous SCYL2 recruitment dynamics and
functions in endocytosis, a key cellular process, within live cells and during neuronal development. This research
will jumpstart the study of the understudied SCYL2 protein associated with the rare disease AMC4 and open
new horizons for further characterization of endocytic proteins and their disease-associated variants during
development.

title: Spatially resolved multiomics profiling of microbes and their host tissue
text:
Microbes such as Bacteria influence the healthiness of their host in many different ways. To understand how
the microbes interact with their host, we need tools to characterize the microbes spatial distribution and also
their cellular status. This project aims to build a widely applicable spatial RNA and protein sequencing platform
to understand microbe status, spatial organization and their interactions with their host.

title: Temporal and Spatial Control of Oligodendrocyte Fate Specification
text:
Proper formation of distinct types of neurons and glial cells in the central nervous system is essential for motor
and intellectual function. The long-term goal of this project is to understand how oligodendrocyte lineage cells,
which includes cells that wrap axons with insulating myelin, are produced by neural progenitors. Completion of
the project aims will substantially extend our understanding of the molecular mechanisms that control formation
of glial cells for myelination.

title: Cell Transitions during Bone Fracture Healing
text:
Failures in bone fracture healing can occur due to disruptions to cellular processes at different phases of the
healing process. This proposal examines cellular fate decisions that occur at different times in the healing
process to produce the tissues that successfully heal the injured bone.

title: Decoding mPFC Plasticity Across Life Stages
text:
The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is a brain region involved in higher functions, such as memory, social
interaction and motivation. Early life experiences shape the development of this important brain area, ultimately
influencing its function in adulthood, yet the critical developmental steps required for normal mPFC maturation
are not clear. The proposed work will use experimental animals, mice, to investigate important mechanisms of
mPFC plasticity, identifying essential developmental steps required to achieve normal function, and explore
strategies to improve function in adulthood.

title: The role of hnRNPK in pancreatic beta cells
text:
The development of hyperglycemia, insulin insufficiency, and beta cell failure all underly the progression to
Type 2 diabetes. Many efforts have been made to improve the lives of those living with T2D including novel
drugs that enhance insulin secretion and induce weight loss but prevalence of this disease is still climbing.
Therefore, it is essential the diabetes research community strives to better understand novel mechanisms
underlying T2D pathology to help lessen the negative impact this disease has on the world.

title: Breast cancer cells secrete glycosylated protein to facilitate blood-brain barrier opening and brain metastasis
text:
Breast cancer brain metastasis is a severe cause of mortality in the United States, and it is not known how
metastatic cancer spreads from the breast to the brain. We have discovered that metastatic breast cancer cells
secrete fetuin-A (FetA), and cancer-derived FetA transiently opens the blood-brain barrier, unlike serum FetA,
and glycosylation on cancer-derived FetA is critical for its function to open the barrier. Our project aims to
investigate the mechanism by which cancer-derived FetA opens the blood-brain barrier to facilitate breast cancer
brain metastasis, with the goal of developing a preventive strategy against breast cancer brain metastasis.

title: Assessing Diffusion MRI Metrics for Detecting Changes of Synaptic Density in Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Alzheimer’s disease affects as many as 5 million individuals over the age of 65 in the United States and 35
million worldwide. The best treatment is prevention, which requires objective diagnostic tools for early
detection. To this end, the proposed research aims to identify novel imaging biomarkers obtained with
magnetic resonance imaging as early differential diagnostic tools.

title: Exploring the Impact of Base Deaminase Deregulation on Precancer Evolution
text:
In 295,000 individuals in the US who are living with myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), progression to therapy
resistant secondary acute myeloid leukemia (sAML) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality as well as
growing healthcare economic burden thereby underscoring the pressing unmet medical need for predicting and
preventing MPN progression. Recently, we discovered that inflammatory cytokine-induced activation of
APOBEC3C and ADAR1p150 base deaminases fuels hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC)
proliferation during leukemic transformation of MPNs. Thus, the overarching goal of this project is to elucidate
the APOBEC3C-mediated DNA and ADAR1p150-mediated RNA editing mechanisms governing MPN HSPC
reprogramming into long-lived, self-renewing leukemia stem cells (LSC) with the ultimate aim of informing the
development of strategies that predict and prevent sAML transformation.

title: dkNET Coordinating Unit: Harnessing the Power of AI and Data Science forCollaborative Discovery and Sharing in the DK Community
text:
Advancing privacy-preserving artificial intelligence (AI) methods will enable researchers to leverage larger, more
diverse diabetes datasets without requiring the sharing of sensitive patient information. By implementing
federated learning across distributed research sites, this project will accelerate collaborative discovery while
maintaining compliance with privacy, ethical, and regulatory requirements. The resulting infrastructure will
improve the development of more accurate and generalizable AI models to better understand, predict, and treat
